365.title: Right speech
365.hook: no lying, no divisive speech, no harsh speech, no idle chatter (MN 117)
365.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists take the fourth precept, not to speak falsely, often reciting it in Pali at the temple; right speech as a path factor adds abstaining from divisive, harsh and idle speech, and monastics keep detailed rules about speech in their discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahimsa, and your line, no harm meant. Did you catch one of those little films before it finished? Day three hundred sixty-five: a calendar year's worth of days on this path.

I'm five minutes away, typed by someone who hasn't left the house yet. A story about a coworker, told while she's out at lunch. A reply with a little edge on it. A long voice memo that could have been one sentence. None of these is a crime. Set side by side, though, they make a fairly complete map of how talk goes wrong, and the Buddha drew that same map in four lines. Right intention was the direction set inside. Today we reach the first factor of the path that comes out of the mouth: right speech.
screen: `I'M FIVE MINUTES AWAY.` → `UNTRUE, ABOUT SOMEONE, SHARP.` → `OR NEVER NEEDED AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Sammā vācā. Sammā: right, whole, complete. Vācā: speech, the voice. In the great forty sutta, the Buddha defines it with four abstentions. Abstaining from false speech. From divisive speech, the kind that splits people apart. From harsh speech. And from idle chatter. Four guards at the door of the mouth. Two things stand out. First, the five precepts lay Buddhists take name only one of these, not lying. Right speech asks for all four. Second, look at the last guard. Idle chatter, samphappalāpa in Pali, is talk that goes nowhere: words to fill a silence, gossip with no purpose, saying things only to be heard. And it sits on the same list as lying. That doesn't make small talk forbidden; many kind words are small. Some teachers put the test as purpose: is this going anywhere good? The same sutta does something else worth noticing. It sets right speech inside a circle. Right view recognizes wrong speech as wrong. Right effort works to let it go. Right mindfulness stays present while you do. So speech isn't mended by a rule alone; three other factors run around it. Why would a path to freedom spend a whole factor on talk? Because speech is where intention, last week's subject, first touches another person. You set the direction inside; now it comes out loud. And talk runs all day long, so the chances to practice do too.
screen: `SAMMĀ VĀCĀ: WHOLE SPEECH.` · `FOUR GUARDS AT THE MOUTH.` · `IDLE CHATTER MAKES THE LIST.` · `THREE FACTORS CIRCLE IT.` · then, large: `FOUR GUARDS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest. Let your mind replay the last day's talk, like scrolling back through your messages. Don't judge it; just sort. Was anything not quite true? Anything said about someone who wasn't there? Anything sharp? Anything said only to fill the quiet? Notice which guard was the sleepiest. Then let the replay go, and rest in the silence for a while, where no words are needed. After the bell, take that sleepy guard with you. The bell holds the time.
Sammā vācā. Right speech: no lying, no divisive words, no harsh words, no idle chatter. The third factor of the path.
Your line: four guards. Today, check your words as they leave: true, uniting, gentle, worth saying. Day three hundred sixty-five.

screen: `DAY 365 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FIVE MARKS OF GOOD SPEECH.`

366.title: Five marks of good speech
366.hook: spoken at the right time, true, gentle, beneficial, with a kind heart (AN 5.198)
366.tomorrow: The stick in the baby's throat
366.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often offer these five as questions to ask before speaking, and monastics hear the same five in the simile of the saw as a training in staying steady when others speak badly to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma vaca, right speech, and your line, four guards. Which guard was the sleepiest when you checked your words? Day three hundred sixty-six.

You've been rehearsing it in the shower for three days. The sentence you need to say to your roommate about the dishes, or to your father about his driving, or to a friend about the thing she keeps doing. Every version you try is either so soft it means nothing, or so sharp it'll start a fight. Long ago, the Buddha gave a checklist for exactly this moment. It has five boxes, and it would fit on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror. Today: five marks of good speech.
screen: `THE SENTENCE IN THE SHOWER.` → `TOO SOFT, OR TOO SHARP.` → `A STICKY NOTE WITH FIVE BOXES.`

segments.voice: In a short sutta in the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha says that speech with five qualities is well spoken, blameless, and not faulted by the wise. Here they are. Spoken at the right time. Spoken truly. Spoken gently. Spoken for benefit. And spoken with a mind of goodwill. Hold your shower sentence up to them and something shifts. Truth isn't first on this list. It's second. Time comes first. A true thing said at the wrong moment, in the middle of the argument, in front of the whole table, at eleven at night, can land like a stone. Gently translates the Pali saṇha: smooth, soft, fine. It's about how the words feel to receive, not only what they say. For benefit means the words are going somewhere good, for the listener, and not only for your own relief. And the last mark isn't about the words at all. It's about the heart they come from: a mind of goodwill. You could say perfectly chosen words with quiet contempt underneath, and this list would catch it. The same five turn up in the simile of the saw from a few days ago, but turned around. There the Buddha lists them as ways other people may speak to you: at the right time or not, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, helpfully or not, with goodwill or with hate. And the training is to stay steady either way. So the list cuts in both directions. It's what to aim for when you speak, and it's not a test everyone else must pass before you'll stay kind.
screen: `FIVE MARKS OF WELL-SPOKEN SPEECH.` · `TIME COMES FIRST.` · `GENTLE, HELPFUL, FROM GOODWILL.` · `THE LIST CUTS BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `TRUE, TIMELY, KIND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring back a sentence you've been rehearsing, or one you'll need to say soon. Let it play once. Now hold it to the five, slowly, a breath or two for each. Is it the right time? Is it true? Is it gentle? Will it help? Is it coming from goodwill? If one box stays empty, don't force it. Just notice which one. Then rest, and let the sentence wait in the quiet until it's ready. The bell holds the time.
Subhasita vaca, well-spoken speech. Timely, true, gentle, beneficial, and from a mind of goodwill. From the Numbered Discourses, in the book of fives.
Your line: true, timely, kind. Before one hard sentence today, ask the five questions, and notice what changes in the sentence. Day three hundred sixty-six.

367.title: The stick in the baby's throat
367.hook: he says what is true and helpful even when unwelcome, at the right time, as you'd pull a stick from a baby's throat (MN 58)
367.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell this story when explaining right speech, and monastic communities have a formal way of pointing out a fellow monastic's fault, raised respectfully and at a suitable time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: subhasita vaca, and your line, true, timely, kind. Did one hard sentence go through all five boxes before it left? Day three hundred sixty-seven.

A prince named Abhaya comes to the Buddha with a trick question someone has coached him to ask. It's built with two prongs, so that either answer sticks in the throat. Would you ever say something that others find unwelcome and disagreeable? If the Buddha says yes, how is he different from anyone else who hurts people's feelings? If he says no, what about the hard things he has said about the monk Devadatta? Abhaya sits down with his baby son on his lap. That small detail turns out to be the whole answer. Today: the stick in the baby's throat.
screen: `A TRICK QUESTION, TWO PRONGS.` → `YES OR NO, IT STICKS.` → `A BABY ON HIS LAP.`

segments.voice: The Buddha doesn't say yes or no. He looks at the baby. Prince, he asks, if this child, through someone's carelessness, put a stick or a pebble in his mouth, what would you do? Abhaya answers at once. I'd get it out. If I couldn't get it out right away, I'd hold his head with my left hand, crook a finger of my right, and pull it out, even if it drew blood. Why? Because I have compassion for the child. That, the Buddha says, is how he speaks. Then he lays out the cases, six of them, like a grid. If something is untrue, or true but of no help, he doesn't say it, whether people would welcome it or not. If it's true and helpful but unwelcome, he knows the right time to say it. If it's true and helpful and welcome, again, he knows the right time. Look at what does the deciding. Whether people will like it is on the grid, but it never settles anything. Wounding them isn't on it at all. The deciding questions are: is it true, does it help? And then: when? The baby holds all of it. Pulling a stick from a child's throat isn't gentle in the moment. There may be crying, even a little blood. But nobody watching would call it cruel, because everyone can see what it's for and who it's for. The sutta ends with Abhaya, who came to trap the Buddha, going for refuge instead. Some sticks come out easily.
screen: `HE LOOKS AT THE BABY.` · `I'D GET IT OUT, EVEN WITH BLOOD.` · `SIX CASES: TRUE, HELPFUL, WHEN.` · `WELCOME NEVER DECIDES.` · then, large: `THE RIGHT TIME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of one true thing someone in your life may need to hear: about their health, their work, a habit that's hurting them. Ask the Buddha's questions. Is it true? Will it help them? Then the hardest one: when? Picture a moment that would be right, when they can hear it, not when you're angry or tired. Picture your hand steady and careful, the way you'd reach for a child. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kala, time. The Buddha's picture for a truth that's unwelcome but needed: said for the other's sake, at the right time.
Your line: the right time. If there's one needed truth today, say it gently, at a moment they can hear it. If that moment isn't today, waiting counts too. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

368.title: The mirror
368.hook: to young Rahula: reflect as in a mirror before speaking or acting (MN 61)
368.howItsDone: Many Buddhists use this teaching as a daily review: reflecting before acting, and in the evening looking back over the day's words and deeds; in monasteries, faults are acknowledged to a fellow monastic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kala, and your line, the right time. Was there a needed truth, and did you find its moment, or wisely wait? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

Late afternoon, at Ambalatthika, near Rajagaha. A boy named Rahula sees his father coming and sets out a seat and a vessel of water for washing feet. The father is the Buddha. Rahula is his son, now a novice monk, and tradition says he was about seven. The Buddha washes his feet and leaves a little water in the bottom of the vessel. Rahula, do you see this little bit of water? Yes, sir. That little, he says, is what's left of the monk's life in anyone who feels no shame telling a deliberate lie. He throws the water away. Then he turns the vessel upside down. Today: the mirror.
screen: `A SEAT AND A VESSEL OF WATER.` → `A LITTLE LEFT IN THE BOTTOM.` → `TURNED UPSIDE DOWN.`

segments.voice: It's a stark start for a seven-year-old, and it begins with lying for a reason: the Buddha says that someone with no shame about a deliberate lie could do any wrong at all. Then he changes the picture. Rahula, what is a mirror for? For reflecting, sir. In the same way, he says, reflect before you do anything with your body, your speech or your mind. Ask: would this lead to harm for me, for others, or for both? If so, don't do it. If not, go ahead. And not only before. Reflect while you're doing it, and stop if you see harm. Reflect afterward too. If a word or deed turned out harmful, he tells his son, reveal it to a teacher or a wise companion, and hold back next time. If it turned out well, be glad, and keep training. For a harmful thought, he adds, be troubled by it and turn away. Before, during, after. Three looks in the mirror, at three doors: body, speech, mind. Notice the tone. There's no threat of punishment. A child is handed a tool, not a lecture, and a mirror is a gentle tool. It doesn't scold. It just shows you your face. The teaching even ends with gladness: when you see you've done well, enjoy it. For speech, the mirror is a pause. One breath between the thought and the sentence, long enough to ask: who will this help, and who could it hurt?
screen: `A MIRROR IS FOR REFLECTING.` · `BEFORE, DURING, AFTER.` · `A TOOL, NOT A LECTURE.` · `THE PAUSE BEFORE THE SENTENCE.` · then, large: `LOOK IN THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Picture a small mirror in your hand. Think of something you're likely to say today: an email, a reply, a comment at dinner. Hold it up to the glass. Will it harm me, them, or both? Breathe. Then think of something you said yesterday, and look again, gently, the way a mirror looks, without scolding. If it went well, let yourself be glad. If it didn't, note it, and set it down. The bell holds the time.
The mirror. The Buddha's tool for his son Rahula: reflect before, during and after acting, in body, speech and mind.
Your line: look in the mirror. Before you speak today, pause for one breath, about as long as a glance in the glass. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

trapdoor: what you thought: reflection means feeling guilty about what you did.
what it means: looking at an act before, during and after, to see whether it harms.

369.title: Not to divide
369.hook: what he hears here he does not repeat there to set people apart (DN 1)
369.howItsDone: Buddhists treat abstaining from divisive speech as part of right speech; monastics keep a rule against tale-bearing among monks, and some teachers suggest simply letting gossip stop with you.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mirror, and your line, look in the mirror. Did one breath slip in between a thought and a sentence? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

It starts so innocently. Can I tell you something? Don't say I said this. And then a sentence moves from one room to another, from one friend to the next, and arrives a little bigger than it left. By the end of the week, two people who used to get lunch together aren't speaking, and neither is quite sure why. It can happen in an office, a family, a group chat. The sutta that opens the Long Discourses has a line about exactly this. Today: not to divide.
screen: `DON'T SAY I SAID THIS.` → `ONE ROOM TO THE NEXT.` → `TWO FRIENDS, NOT SPEAKING.`

segments.voice: The sutta is the Brahmajala, the all-embracing net, and near its start it lists what an ordinary person might praise in the Buddha. Several of the items are about speech. One is about pisuṇā vācā, divisive speech, the second of the four guards from a few days ago. And the description is precise. What he hears in one place, he doesn't repeat in another to set people there against the people here. What he hears there, he doesn't repeat here. That's the mechanism of gossip, named exactly. Information isn't the problem. Carrying it in order to split people is. The sutta doesn't stop at refusing. It turns the guard into a job. In T. W. Rhys Davids's translation, he lives "as a binder together of those who are divided, an encourager of those who are friends". The passage goes on to call him a peacemaker who speaks words that make for peace. So this guard has two halves. Don't carry the sentence that splits. And when you can, carry the sentence that mends. Notice how ordinary this is. No vows, no robes. Just what you do with something you heard by the coffee machine. And notice what it does over time. Over time, people tend to notice who repeats things, and who doesn't. The tradition takes it seriously enough to put it in two places: here on the path, and in the monks' own code, which has a specific offense for tale-bearing between monks.
screen: `PISUṆĀ VĀCĀ: SPEECH THAT SPLITS.` · `HEARD HERE, NOT REPEATED THERE.` · `A BINDER TOGETHER.` · `THE ONE OTHERS TRUST.` · then, large: `NOT TO DIVIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of something you heard recently about someone, the kind of thing that travels. Notice the small pull to pass it on, maybe a little buzz in the chest. Don't fight it. Just feel it, and let it sit there. Then think of the two people it would land between, and picture them still speaking, still getting lunch. Rest in the quiet of a sentence not carried. The bell holds the time.
Pisuna vaca, divisive speech. In the first of the Long Discourses, the Buddha doesn't carry words to split people; he binds together those who are divided.
Your line: a sentence that mends. Today, refuse one piece of gossip, and if you can, carry one sentence that mends. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

370.title: Speak or be silent
370.hook: when together, talk about the teaching or keep noble silence (MN 26)
370.howItsDone: Many Buddhist retreats keep noble silence for their whole length, with talk only for teaching interviews and practical needs; some monasteries keep silence at meals or through the night until morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pisuna vaca, and your line, a sentence that mends. Did one piece of gossip stop with you, and did any sentence mend something? Day three hundred seventy.

Evening, outside a hermitage near Savatthi. The Buddha is standing at a closed door, waiting. Inside, a group of his monks are deep in conversation about the teaching. He could walk straight in. They'd stop mid-sentence and bow, and the whole room would turn toward him. Instead he stays on the step, in the evening light, and lets them finish. Only when the talk has come to its end does he clear his throat and knock. It's a quiet moment, and it opens a long sutta. Today: speak or be silent.
screen: `A TEACHER AT THE DOOR.` → `HE LETS THEM FINISH.` → `THEN HE KNOCKS.`

segments.voice: The sutta is the Noble Search, in the Middle Length Discourses. The monks had been hoping to hear a talk from the Buddha himself, and Ananda brought him to the hermitage of a brahmin named Rammaka, where they were gathered. When the door opens, the Buddha sits down, asks what they were discussing, and approves. Then he gives them a rule of thumb short enough to remember for life. When you gather together, he says, do one of two things: discuss the teaching, or keep noble silence. That's all. Two options, and everything else falls away. Notice what this does to idle chatter, the fourth guard from earlier this week. It isn't fought with a ban. It's crowded out. If you're not talking about what matters, you can simply be quiet together, and that quiet has a name: ariya tuṇhībhāva, noble silence. Not sulking, not awkwardness, not waiting for your turn to talk. A chosen stillness, shared. Elsewhere in the canon, Moggallana gives noble silence a deeper meaning: a level of meditation where even thinking falls still. Modern retreats borrow the phrase for days spent without talking at all. Both point the same direction. And look at what the Buddha does before he says any of it. He doesn't interrupt a good conversation, even one he could improve. He waits outside. Then he speaks. The sutta that follows is long, and full of his own story: leaving home, his teachers, his awakening. It begins with a man waiting quietly on a step.
screen: `TWO OPTIONS WHEN YOU GATHER.` · `CROWDING OUT THE CHATTER.` · `NOBLE SILENCE, CHOSEN TOGETHER.` · `FIRST, HE WAITS OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `SPEAK OR BE SILENT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For these two minutes, practice the second option. The voice in your head may keep talking, but you don't have to answer it. Notice how much of it is chatter: rehearsing, commenting, narrating. Each time you catch it, come back to the breath, the way you'd step back into a quiet room. Then choose an hour later today for noble silence: no talk that isn't needed. The bell holds the time.
Ariya tunhibhava, noble silence. The Buddha's rule for gathering: talk about what matters, or keep noble silence.
Your line: a chosen stillness, shared. Today, keep one silent hour, messages included, and notice what you didn't miss. Day three hundred seventy.

371.title: Right action
371.hook: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct (MN 117)
371.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists commonly take the five precepts, which include the three abstentions of right action, often reciting them in Pali at the temple; ordained monks and nuns keep a fuller discipline that includes celibacy, and traditionally carry a water strainer among their few requisites.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ariya tunhibhava, and your line, a chosen stillness, shared. Did you find a silent hour, and what did you notice you didn't miss? Day three hundred seventy-one, the end of the week.

Tradition gives a Buddhist monk a short list of things to own: robes, a bowl, a razor, a needle, a belt. And one more item that's easy to miss: a water strainer, a small cloth for filtering drinking water. It isn't there for hygiene. It's there so the monk doesn't swallow, and kill, the tiny creatures living in the water. A whole way of life where even a drink of water is done carefully enough to spare something you can barely see. That's how far one factor of the path reaches. Today: right action.
screen: `THREE ROBES, A BOWL, A RAZOR.` → `AND A WATER STRAINER.` → `EVEN A DRINK, DONE CAREFULLY.`

segments.voice: Sammā kammanta. Sammā you know by now: right, whole. Kammanta is action, the work of the body, from the same family as the word kamma. In the great forty sutta, the Buddha defines it with three abstentions: from killing living beings, from taking what isn't given, and from sexual misconduct. If those sound familiar, they should. They're the first three of the five precepts, now standing inside the path. For monks and nuns the third becomes full celibacy; for lay people it means not causing harm through sex, not betraying a partner, not exploiting anyone. The first sutta of the Long Discourses, the one from two days ago, describes the same ground as a way of living rather than a list of rules. The Buddha has laid aside the stick and the sword, it says, and lives with care for every living thing, taking only what's given, and waiting for it to be given. That's the shift worth noticing. Right action isn't only a fence of not-doing. It's a way of moving through the world carefully, the way you carry a sleeping child in from the car. Hands that don't grab. Feet that look where they step. And the circle from right speech is here too: right view sees harmful action as harmful, right effort turns away from it, right mindfulness stays awake while it happens. Look back at the week. Four guards. True, timely, kind. The right time. Look in the mirror. Not to divide. Speak or be silent. A whole week on the mouth. Now the body joins in.
screen: `KAMMANTA: THE WORK OF THE BODY.` · `THREE ABSTENTIONS.` · `STICK AND SWORD LAID ASIDE.` · `MOVING THROUGH THE WORLD CAREFULLY.` · then, large: `ACT WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and feel your hands resting. These hands will do dozens of things today: open doors, type, carry, cook, touch someone. Choose one action you'll do soon, something ordinary, like making a cup of tea. Rehearse it in your mind, slowly, with great care: how you'll lift, pour, set down, as if everything you touch could feel it. Then let the hands rest again, and notice how much care they already know how to hold. The bell holds the time.
Sammā kammanta. Right action: not killing, not taking what isn't given, no sexual misconduct. The fourth factor of the path.
Your line: act with care. Today, do one ordinary action with great care, as if whatever you touch could feel it. Day three hundred seventy-one, and the week is done.

a monk's few possessions traditionally include a water strainer
it filters out tiny creatures so they aren't swallowed.
for monks and nuns, the third abstention means celibacy
for lay people it means no sexual misconduct; ordained people give up sex entirely.

fork.setup: you're a monk on a hot day. the only water nearby is a pond full of tiny living things. what does the monastic life give you for this?
options: drink it anyway; you're thirsty.
go without water all day.
a cloth water strainer.
fork.reveal: a water strainer is one of a monk's traditional requisites, so the tiny creatures aren't swallowed. care reaches even a drink of water.

original.note: Pali sammā kammanta: right action, the fourth factor of the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: right action means following rules.
what it means: acting with care: not killing, not taking, no sexual misconduct, and moving through the world gently.
what a scholar hears: kammanta comes from the same verbal root as kamma, to do; MN 117 defines it by three abstentions that overlap the first three of the five precepts.
